title: Anaphylaxis / STEMI / DKA / Stroke / Suicidal OD / First-episode psychosis

2.title: Anaphylaxis with airway compromise
2.stem:
Patient: 27-year-old male.
History: Known IgE-mediated peanut allergy with prior anaphylaxis; carries epinephrine auto-injector. 20 minutes after eating takeout labeled peanut-free, developed diffuse pruritus, facial swelling, throat tightness, and wheezing. Used one 0.3 mg epinephrine auto-injector IM in the thigh with only partial improvement. On arrival, progressive dyspnea and lightheadedness. Takes propranolol 40 mg BID for migraine prophylaxis. No asthma diagnosis. No recent ACE inhibitor.
Physical Examination: Distressed, biphasic stridor, lip and tongue angioedema, widespread urticaria. BP 78/46 mmHg, HR 128 bpm, RR 32, SpO2 88% on room air improving to 92% on non-rebreather. Diffuse wheezes. Capillary refill 4 s. Alert but anxious.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Fingerstick glucose 102 mg/dL. Point-of-care lactate 3.8 mmol/L. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Portable chest X-ray pending. Serum tryptase drawn (result pending). ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 48 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg on NRB.
2.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Anaphylaxis (severe) with airway involvement (stridor, angioedema), bronchospasm, and distributive/hypotensive shock after probable peanut exposure; partial response to one IM epinephrine dose; beta-blocker therapy may contribute to refractory features. Top differential: acute severe asthma exacerbation (less likely as primary without asthma history and with urticaria/hypotension/angioedema), hereditary/acquired angioedema (no urticaria/hypotension typical), foreign-body airway obstruction, sepsis with laryngitis (tempo and urticaria argue against).

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Do not delay epinephrine/airway for labs. Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring; repeat vitals frequently; prepare for definitive airway. ABG/VBG as available; lactate; ECG already done; chest X-ray after stabilization if indicated; serum tryptase (ideally within ~1–3 h of onset, already drawn) for later confirmation; document allergen exposure for outpatient allergy follow-up.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical — treat as airway/breathing/circulation emergency now. Red flags: biphasic stridor, tongue/floor-of-mouth swelling, hypoxia with rising PaCO2, refractory hypotension, altered mentation, cardiac arrest risk, need for repeat epinephrine or escalation to airway.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Give IM epinephrine immediately into the anterolateral thigh; do not wait for IV access, antihistamines, or steroids. Antihistamines/steroids are adjuncts only — never first-line for airway/shock. Avoid relying on a single auto-injector if shock/airway persists — repeat IM epinephrine q3–5 min as needed. Patient is on propranolol: expect possible refractory hypotension/bronchospasm; if shock persists after epinephrine and fluids, consider IM/IV glucagon per protocol. Caution with IV epinephrine boluses in conscious patients (use monitored infusion if needed for refractory shock). Prepare early for difficult airway (angioedema) — most experienced airway operator, backup surgical airway. Observe for biphasic reaction after stabilization.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Immediate IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) anterolateral thigh; high-flow O2; large-bore IV access; rapid crystalloid bolus for hypotension; nebulized epinephrine and/or bronchodilator for lower-airway wheeze if needed; early airway decision if stridor/angioedema progresses; H1 antihistamine and corticosteroid as adjuncts after epinephrine; glucagon if beta-blocker–refractory shock; stop allergen exposure; ICU/monitored observation for biphasic anaphylaxis; prescribe ≥2 epinephrine auto-injectors and urgent allergy referral on discharge planning.

3.title: STEMI
3.stem:
Patient: 61-year-old male.
History: Long-standing type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. Smokes 1 pack/day. Awoke at 05:30 with crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw, associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Pain ongoing for 90 minutes. No prior MI. Takes metformin and atorvastatin.
Physical Examination: Anxious, diaphoretic. BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 104 bpm regular, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air. Heart sounds S1/S2, no murmur. Lungs clear. No calf swelling.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Troponin I elevated at 2.4 ng/mL (URL 0.04). ECG: 3 mm ST-segment elevation in V2–V4 with reciprocal ST depression in II, III, aVF. Chest X-ray: no acute pulmonary edema.
3.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), anterior wall (LAD territory), Killip I; ongoing ischemic chest pain ~90 minutes. Top differential: unstable angina/NSTEMI with early ST changes, aortic dissection with coronary involvement (less likely without tearing/back pain or pulse deficit), myopericarditis, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Continuous cardiac monitoring; serial ECGs if symptoms change; repeat high-sensitivity troponin (does not delay reperfusion); basic metabolic panel, CBC, coagulation panel for cath; activate emergent coronary angiography / primary PCI pathway; CXR already done.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical / time-critical emergency — activate cath lab / STEMI pathway immediately (door-to-balloon target). Red flags: hypotension, acute heart failure/pulmonary edema, malignant arrhythmias (VT/VF), complete heart block, refractory pain, cardiogenic shock.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not delay reperfusion for nonessential testing or troponin confirmation. Caution with nitrates if hypotensive or RV infarct suspected (inferior pattern not primary here). Dual antiplatelet and anticoagulation per protocol before/during PCI. Watch for arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock. Hold metformin around contrast if AKI risk.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Aspirin (chewed) and P2Y12 / anticoagulation per local ACS–PCI protocol; oxygen only if hypoxemic; urgent primary PCI; ICU/CCU monitoring post-PCI; smoking cessation and secondary prevention counseling after stabilization.

4.title: DKA
4.stem:
Patient: 22-year-old female.
History: Known type 1 diabetes on insulin pump. 3 days of polyuria, polydipsia, and progressive nausea after a viral illness. Missed several bolus corrections. Today: vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy. No fever reported at home.
Physical Examination: Ill-appearing, dry mucous membranes. BP 96/60, HR 122, RR 28 with Kussmaul breathing, SpO2 98% RA, temp 37.1°C. Abdomen soft, diffusely tender without peritonitis. Fruity breath odor noted.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Glucose 482 mg/dL. VBG: pH 7.12, HCO3 8 mmol/L, anion gap 28. Serum ketones positive (beta-hydroxybutyrate elevated). K+ 5.6 mEq/L, Na 132, Cr 1.4 (baseline 0.7). WBC 14.2. Urinalysis: glucose 4+, ketones 3+.
4.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Diabetic ketoacidosis (moderate–severe) precipitated by intercurrent illness / insulin omission; volume depletion; high anion-gap metabolic acidosis with ketonemia. Top differential: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (less likely with prominent ketosis/acidosis in young T1D), starvation ketosis with stress hyperglycemia, primary acute abdomen with secondary metabolic derangement.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Fingerstick/serum glucose trending; serial VBG or ABG; electrolytes q2–4h especially potassium; beta-hydroxybutyrate; CBC; cultures if infection suspected; ECG given hyperkalemia; consider lipase if abdominal pain remains atypical after resuscitation.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: High/critical — start IV fluids and DKA protocol promptly; admit to ICU/step-down capable of frequent labs. Red flags: K <3.3 before insulin, deteriorating mental status (cerebral edema risk), refractory shock, severe hypokalemia during treatment.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not start insulin if potassium is <3.3 mEq/L—replete first. Monitor for cerebral edema (young adult). Avoid overly rapid sodium/osmolality shifts. Transition off insulin pump carefully. Maintain VTE risk awareness.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Isotonic fluid resuscitation then protocolized IV insulin infusion after potassium safety check; add dextrose when glucose falls to protocol threshold (~200–250 mg/dL); electrolyte repletion; identify/treat trigger; diabetes education and pump review before discharge.

5.title: Acute ischemic stroke
5.stem:
Patient: 72-year-old female.
History: Atrial fibrillation on apixaban (last dose this morning uncertain per family). Sudden-onset right-sided weakness and aphasia witnessed at 10:15. Arrives ED at 11:05 (50 minutes from onset). Hypertension, prior TIA.
Physical Examination: BP 178/98, HR 96 irregularly irregular, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, glucose 118 mg/dL. NIHSS 12: right hemiparesis, expressive aphasia, right facial droop. No seizure activity.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Non-contrast head CT: no hemorrhage. CTA head/neck pending. INR 1.1, creatinine 0.9, platelets normal.
5.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute ischemic stroke with disabling deficits (aphasia + hemiparesis), last known well 10:15; atrial fibrillation with possible cardioembolic source; no ICH on non-contrast CT. Top differential: seizure with Todd’s paresis (no witnessed seizure), intracranial hemorrhage (excluded on NCCT), hypoglycemia (glucose normal), complex migraine (less likely with AF and NIHSS 12).

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Immediate NCCT (done); CTA head/neck ± CT perfusion per protocol; labs for thrombolysis/thrombectomy eligibility; ECG/telemetry; swallow screen before oral intake.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical / hyperacute — stroke code; door-to-needle and endovascular decision within time windows; do not delay vascular imaging. Red flags: declining consciousness, airway compromise, hemorrhagic transformation signs, severe hypertension outside protocol targets.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Confirm anticoagulation / last apixaban dose before IV thrombolysis. Respect BP targets per protocol. Keep NPO until swallow cleared. Fall and aspiration precautions. Avoid hypotonic fluids.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: If eligible, IV thrombolysis and/or endovascular thrombectomy pathway; admit to stroke unit; time restart/optimization of anticoagulation after follow-up imaging; secondary prevention and early rehab.

6.title: Suicidal crisis with suspected TCA/SSRI overdose
6.stem:
Patient: 29-year-old female.
History: Major depression on amitriptyline 75 mg at bedtime and sertraline 100 mg daily. Partner found her unresponsive-appearing after she sent goodbye texts stating she intended to die and had taken "a lot of my nerve pills." Empty amitriptyline bottle nearby (≈60 × 25 mg missing); sertraline bottle also depleted. Time of ingestion uncertain (~1–3 hours). No known seizure. Prior suicide attempt 2 years ago. No alcohol co-ingestion reported.
Physical Examination: Awake but drowsy, tearful, cooperative when engaged. BP 98/62, HR 118 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, temp 37.0°C. Pupils midsize, sluggish. Dry mucous membranes. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. No focal neurologic deficit. Skin warm, no rigidity. 1:1 sitter at bedside; belongings searched.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Fingerstick glucose 94 mg/dL. ECG: sinus tachycardia 118; QRS 118 ms; QTc 490 ms; no definite Brugada-like pattern yet. VBG: pH 7.36, HCO3 22. Na 138, K 3.9, Cr 0.8. Acetaminophen and salicylate levels pending. Serum ethanol pending. Urine toxicology immunoassay pending. Pregnancy test negative.
6.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute suicidal crisis with intentional overdose — likely amitriptyline (TCA) ± sertraline (SSRI) co-ingestion; early cardiotoxicity signals (sinus tachycardia, QRS widening toward ≥100–120 ms, QTc prolongation). Concurrent high acute suicide risk (intent, plan, goodbye texts, means). Top differential: isolated SSRI overdose/serotonin toxicity (less likely as sole driver without clonus/hyperreflexia/hyperthermia yet), mixed polypharmacy OD, primary arrhythmia/syncope mimic, medical clearance vs primary psychiatric presentation only (do not skip toxicologic/cardiac evaluation).

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial ECGs (QRS/QTc trend); repeat electrolytes (especially K/Mg); acetaminophen and salicylate levels (co-ingestions); ethanol; pregnancy already done; consider ABG if deteriorating; urine tox as adjunct only (does not rule out TCA). Do not delay decontamination/antidote decisions for immunoassay. Psychiatry consult after medical stabilization pathway initiated; collateral for remaining pills/time course.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical — simultaneous medical toxicology emergency and behavioral health emergency. Red flags: QRS ≥100–120 ms or widening, ventricular arrhythmias, seizures, declining GCS/airway risk, hypotension, rising QTc, hyperthermia/clonus suggesting serotonin toxicity, elopement or further self-harm attempts.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Maintain 1:1 observation and ligature-free environment; do not leave unattended for "psych only" disposition before medical clearance. For TCA toxicity: sodium bicarbonate for wide QRS / Na-channel blockade per ACLS/tox guidance; avoid class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics and avoid physostigmine; caution with antipsychotics that further prolong QTc until ECG stabilizes. Do not induce emesis. Activated charcoal only if early presentation, protected airway, and no contraindications. Avoid premature psychiatric ward transfer with unstable ECG. Screen for ongoing intent/plan; remove means.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: ABCs + continuous telemetry; IV access; treat wide-complex TCA cardiotoxicity with IV sodium bicarbonate boluses/infusion targeting narrowing QRS per protocol; correct electrolytes; benzodiazepines first-line for seizures; early airway if GCS falls. Poison control / toxicology involvement. Serial ECGs and observation for delayed TCA deterioration. Parallel suicide precautions (1:1, search, no sharps). After medical clearance criteria met, urgent psychiatry for involuntary hold assessment as indicated, safety planning, and antidepressant regimen revision (avoid unsupervised TCA restart).

7.title: First-episode psychosis vs delirium
7.stem:
Patient: 24-year-old male.
History: No prior psychiatric diagnosis. Over 5 days, family reports new auditory hallucinations (commenting voices), paranoid delusions that neighbors implanted a chip, severe insomnia, and agitation. Yesterday he was found wandering outside at night, disoriented to time. Today in ED he is intermittently inattentive and keeps falling asleep mid-sentence, then abruptly becomes fearful and tries to leave. No known drug use per family, but friends mention possible stimulant use at a party 1 week ago. Mild feverish feeling at home. No head trauma witnessed. Takes no medications.
Physical Examination: BP 148/90, HR 110, RR 20, SpO2 98% RA, temp 38.1°C. Appears ill/tired. Mucous membranes dry. Pupils midsize reactive. Neck supple (limited cooperation). Intermittent attention, fluctuating orientation; briefly follows commands then distractible. No frank focal motor deficit. Mild tremor. Skin: no diaphoresis/rigidity of NMS; no clear clonus. Agitated when approached; security present.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Glucose 108 mg/dL. Na 148, K 3.6, Cr 1.3, WBC 13.8, CK 420. AST/ALT mildly up. Urine tox immunoassay pending. Ethanol negative. ECG: sinus tach 110, QTc 445 ms. Non-contrast head CT pending. LP not done.
7.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute encephalopathy with psychotic features — must treat as first-episode psychosis vs delirium/organic secondary psychosis until proven otherwise. Red flags for medical/delirium/tox cause: subacute-to-acute 5-day course, fluctuating attention/arousal, fever, tachycardia, possible stimulant exposure, mild metabolic derangement. Primary first-episode schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis remains on the differential but should not short-circuit medical workup. Top differential: stimulant/other intoxication or withdrawal, CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis), autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic encephalopathy, intracranial mass/bleed (less likely without focal signs), primary psychiatric first-episode psychosis.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Fingerstick/serum glucose (done); BMP, CBC, LFTs, CK already started — add TSH, B12 as available; urine and appropriately timed serum toxicology; ECG (done). Non-contrast head CT now given altered/fluctuating mentation + new psychosis. Low threshold for LP after imaging if fever/encephalitic features persist (CNS infection/autoimmune workup). Consider EEG if nonconvulsive seizures suspected. Do not rely on "psych clearance" labs alone when delirium flags present.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: High/critical — medical workup and safety stabilization before assuming primary psychiatry. Red flags: progressive fever/meningismus, seizures, declining GCS, severe agitation with violence risk, hyperthermia/rigidity (NMS/serotonin), focal neuro deficits, inability to protect airway.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not sedate heavily and discharge to psych without addressing delirium/tox/CNS infection possibilities. Avoid premature high-dose antipsychotic monotherapy as the only intervention while fever/fluctuating attention remain unexplained. Use least restrictive safe environment; protect patient and staff from elopement/assault. Caution with QTc-prolonging agents and anticholinergic burden in possible toxidromes. If encephalitis suspected, do not delay LP/imaging for involuntary psych admission paperwork.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Parallel tracks: (1) medical — CT, labs/tox, consider LP ± acyclovir if encephalitis cannot be excluded, IV fluids, treat identifiable metabolic triggers; (2) safety — quiet room, continuous observation, verbal de-escalation, offer PO antipsychotic/benzo only as needed for dangerous agitation after ECG/tox context considered, IM options per protocol if imminent violence; (3) psychiatry consult for first-episode pathway once life-threatening medical causes addressed or co-managed. Document capacity/hold status; arrange medical admission (medicine/neuro) preferentially over pure psych ward if delirium/organic workup ongoing.
